title: The Siege of Global Energy: Houthis Take Bab al-Mandab, Saudi Pipeline Falls, Oil Tops $100 as the IAEA Refers Iran to the Security Council
subhead: In a single week the Iran war stopped being a shipping war and became a geography war: Houthis seized Mokha and Perim Island to command Bab al-Mandab, a drone strike launched from Iraqi soil forced Saudi Arabia to shut its East-West pipeline, and Brent crossed $100 for the first time since July. In parallel the IAEA referred Iran's nuclear file to the UN Security Council for the first time in 20 years and revealed a new North Korean enrichment plant — the non-proliferation framework fracturing just as the energy map closes in.

sections.heading: The Chokepoints Fall One by One: Houthis Take the Coast, Riyadh Shuts the Pipeline
sections.body:
What began the week as a Red Sea skirmish ended it as a structural stranglehold on Gulf energy. On Monday the Houthis were still trading drone and missile strikes with Saudi Arabia; by Thursday they had seized the strategic port of Mokha, about 80km north of Bab al-Mandab, and by Saturday they had rolled up an estimated 130km (81 miles) of Yemen's Red Sea coastline and captured Perim Island, the rocky outcrop that guards the strait's narrowest point. Yemeni government forces withdrew from Perim and Mokha without holding, and the Iran-backed group now stands astride the southern gateway between the Indian Ocean, the Red Sea and the Suez Canal.

The same week, the land alternative failed. A drone attack launched from Iraq's Maysan province — which borders Iran — struck Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline, the 1,200km overland line carrying an estimated 4-5% of global oil supply as a Hormuz bypass, forcing Riyadh to shut it and hold off on retaliation following a call from Iraq's prime minister. Chatham House fellow Farea al-Muslimi told the BBC that Iran, directly and through proxies, now holds sway over both Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab, chokepoints that together cover more than 35% of global fuel and oil trade. The UN says at least 76,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since July, a figure that quadrupled in the past week.
sections.whyItMatters: Territorial control is a more durable lever over shipping than hit-and-run attacks. With Hormuz already effectively shut, knocking out the Saudi overland bypass and handing Tehran the gateway islands to Bab al-Mandab closes the region's escape routes from two directions at once — and hands Iran a permanent grip on global energy transit, not a temporary disruption.

sections.heading: Oil Tops $100 as the Economic War Tightens Around Tehran
sections.body:
Brent crude crossed $100 a barrel on Wednesday, up 2.83%, the first time since July, after a night in which the US said it destroyed five Iranian oil tankers — four in the Gulf of Oman and one near Kharg Island — while Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed hits on eight tankers and two warships and fired missile barrages at US targets in Jordan. Before the war began in February, Brent traded near $70; the effective closure of Hormuz, through which some 20% of the world's oil and LNG normally passes, has driven the sustained premium. Diesel prices are at record highs and Pakistan's pump prices have crossed 400 rupees a litre.

Washington's economic campaign intensified in parallel. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has described the effort as an 'economic D-Day' to shut down sanctions-evasion channels, and the administration imposed fresh sanctions on more than two dozen Iranian airlines plus foreign cargo providers. The pressure was showing: Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, unseen in public since the February strike that killed his father, issued a written statement urging officials to avoid 'discouraging statements,' while President Masoud Pezeshkian acknowledged Iranian trade has plunged 25-35 percent, the rial has crashed to about 2.2 million per US dollar, and inflation is above 80 percent.
sections.whyItMatters: The war's costs are now compounding: energy above $100 hits importers worldwide at the same moment Washington tightens the financial noose on Tehran. For the White House, rising fuel prices are becoming a political problem ahead of the November midterms, even as there is no visible off-ramp in a conflict now more than six months old.

sections.heading: The Nuclear Files Resurface: Iran Referred to the Security Council, North Korea Builds a New Plant
sections.body:
In a formal escalation running parallel to the military war, the IAEA board of governors referred Iran's nuclear file to the UN Security Council for the first time in 20 years, over non-compliance with its Non-Proliferation Treaty obligations — citing a lack of information on Iran's nuclear stockpile and the absence of IAEA access since strikes during the June 2025 conflict and again in the war that began on 28 February. Iran had roughly 440kg of 60% enriched uranium at the start of the latest war, material that can be enriched relatively quickly toward the 90% weapons-grade threshold. The resolution, tabled by the UK, France, Germany and the US, passed 23-8 with abstentions; China, Russia and Niger voted against.

Days later the watchdog revealed it had identified a new two-storey uranium enrichment facility at North Korea's Yongbyon complex and an expanded annex near Kangson, a development Reuters said could add several warheads' worth of fissile material a year. IAEA chief Rafael Grossi called both developments a 'serious concern.' Kim Jong Un, who visited a 'newly inaugurated nuclear materials production factory' in June, has praised the country's 'greatly expanded production capacity.' Together the two files show the non-proliferation framework deteriorating on both fronts just as the world's attention is consumed by war.
sections.whyItMatters: Both major non-proliferation files are degrading simultaneously. The practical effect of the Iran referral is likely limited — China and Russia hold vetoes, so new sanctions are improbable — but the symbolic weight is real, and North Korea's quietly expanding fissile capacity underscores that today's conflicts rest on unresolved atomic vulnerabilities.

sections.heading: The Air War Over Ukraine Changes Qualitatively, and Kyiv Faces Its Toughest Winter
sections.body:
Russia has shifted to faster, jet-powered Geran drones that cruise at over 300mph, outrunning Kyiv's interceptors and eroding an interception rate that once reached 94% for long-range drones. Ukrainian military figures put jet-powered drone attacks at 350 in June, 1,600 in July and 2,800 in August, with the new munitions outnumbering older models in five nightly attacks; Ukrainian intelligence says some engines are sourced from China. The shift is visible on the ground: a daytime Russian drone strike on a shopping mall in Pavlohrad killed five and wounded 67 including eight children, the third mall attack within days after strikes in Zaporizhzhia and Sumy.

A senior UN official told the BBC that Ukraine faces its 'toughest winter since the 2022 invasion,' a 'race against the clock' to repair a power network being systematically targeted by attacks that 'very deliberately' hit civilian energy infrastructure, transmission lines and shopping centres, with temperatures capable of reaching -20C. Kyiv is enduring more daily air raid alerts than at any time since the 2022 invasion. The escalation broke even a brief agreement to pause strikes on capitals while US envoys visited Moscow and Kyiv, and the drone war is spilling beyond Ukraine's borders — Moldova's prime minister confirmed 17 drones struck Moldovan territory in August alone, more than during all of last year.
sections.whyItMatters: The energy war is becoming the decisive front of the Russia-Ukraine conflict this winter. A faster, harder-to-intercept drone fleet is designed to break civilian resilience precisely as temperatures fall, and the humanitarian stakes could sharpen international pressure on both Moscow and Western allies to push harder for a negotiated outcome.

sections.heading: Alliances Strain on Every Side: Trump's Irish Remark, the UK-Israel Rupture, and a US-Canada Trade War That Keeps Escalating
sections.body:
The week was a study in Western alliance friction. On a two-day trip to Dublin, Donald Trump said Irish unification would 'eventually' happen, a remark that became the day's main transatlantic headline even as officials insisted US policy had not changed — a signal aimed as much at the Irish-American voting bloc before the midterms as at Dublin. Earlier, the UK, France and Canada sanctioned Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, with Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband accusing Israel of 'ethnic cleansing'; Israel responded by shutting the UK's consulate in East Jerusalem and banning 11 British MPs, including Jeremy Corbyn and Diane Abbott, with the BBC describing British-Israeli relations at their lowest ebb in decades.

Across the Atlantic, the US-Canada trade war moved beyond tariffs into outright import bans. Washington banned Canadian dairy, spirits and motorcycles, and threatened to bar Bombardier from the US market unless it moved manufacturing there — this after Canada imposed retaliatory tariffs on about $20bn of US goods. Analysts noted the import ban covers just 0.25% of Canada's exports to the US, suggesting the measures are aimed at inflicting economic pain rather than raising revenue. Trump's pressure has so far consolidated Canadian nationalism behind Prime Minister Mark Carney rather than extracting concessions.
sections.whyItMatters: Washington is simultaneously straining relations with London (over Ireland and the Iran campaign), with Ottawa (over trade and sovereignty), and with Israel (whose settlements policy now faces Western sanctions), even as it fights a war on Iran. Alliance cohesion is being tested on multiple fronts at once, complicating any coordinated response to the energy and nuclear crises.

sections.heading: Iraq Enters the Crossfire, and AI Weapons Targeting Goes Commercial
sections.body:
Two quieter developments point to how the conflict is widening. The drone strikes that forced Saudi Arabia to shut its East-West Pipeline were launched from Iraqi territory — the first time Gulf territory has been hit from Iraqi soil, thrusting Baghdad into an escalation it had tried to stay out of. Iraq's prime minister dismissed a senior military commander in Maysan province and ordered a probe, but the episode complicates the US-Iraq relationship just as Baghdad declared a September 30 US withdrawal 'final.'

Separately, Anthropic disclosed that accounts linked to Iran used its Claude AI to compile targeting data on US Navy warships in the Middle East, and that Iranian, Houthi, Russian and Chinese-linked actors used the model in attempts to develop weapons, run cyber operations and conduct influence campaigns. It is the first public, named case of an American frontier AI model being weaponized against American military forces, and it collapses the barrier to AI-enabled targeting that previously required dedicated state programs.
sections.whyItMatters: The conflict is no longer contained to its original theaters. Iraq's emergence as a launch point against Gulf energy infrastructure complicates any US-Saudi response, while the Anthropic disclosure signals that off-the-shelf commercial AI is now a dual-use accelerant in the targeting arms race — sharpening debates in Washington and Brussels over export controls and model safety.

bottomLine: The week's defining movement is that the Iran war transformed from a shipping war into a geography war. Houthi seizure of Mokha and Perim Island, compounded by the Iraqi-launched drone strike that forced Saudi Arabia to shut the East-West pipeline, closed down the Gulf's energy escape routes from two directions at once — pushing oil above $100 and handing Tehran strategic leverage over two of the world's most vital chokepoints. The non-proliferation framework fractured in parallel, with the IAEA referring Iran to the UN Security Council for the first time in 20 years and revealing a new North Korean enrichment plant, while Russia's shift to faster jet-powered drones set up Ukraine's toughest winter yet. None of the core conflicts showed an off-ramp. Going forward, the watchword is compounding: every closure of a route, every escalation of a nuclear file, and every alliance strain raises the energy and political cost of a war that keeps widening in geography, technology and participation rather than de-escalating. Expect rising fuel prices to dominate domestic politics, sustained scrutiny of AI-enabled targeting, and pressure on Washington to find a settlement before the chokehold on global energy becomes permanent.
sources: BBC, Reuters, AP, Al Jazeera, Fortune, Wall Street Journal, Axios, New York Times, Times of Israel, Navy Times, Al-Monitor, Iran International, Middle East Eye, CNN, Fox News
